subtopic: Distinguish stimulus strength from action-potential amplitude in a single recovered motor axon.
prompt: Intracellular recordings are made from one healthy motor axon. Two brief stimuli, separated by complete recovery, are both above threshold; the second stimulus is stronger. Which change should be expected in the propagated response?

A larger peak action-potential amplitude after the stronger stimulus
A longer absolute refractory period in direct proportion to stimulus strength
A larger sodium concentration gradient established by the stronger stimulus

subtopic: Separate rapid spike generation from the longer-term maintenance of ionic gradients.
prompt: The sodium-potassium pump in an isolated motor axon is suddenly inhibited, but ionic gradients are initially unchanged. Why can several action potentials still occur?

prompt: At a skeletal-muscle membrane potential of -80 mV, take E_Na = +60 mV and E_K = -90 mV. If channels for both cations are open, which pair correctly describes their electrochemical driving forces, V_m - E_ion, and net flux directions?

options.text: Na+: +140 mV, outward; K+: -10 mV, inward
Na+: -20 mV, inward; K+: -170 mV, inward
Na+: +60 mV, outward; K+: -90 mV, inward
Na+: -140 mV, inward; K+: +10 mV, outward

explanation: For a cation, negative V_m-E_ion favors inward flux and positive favors outward flux: -80-60=-140 mV and -80-(-90)=+10 mV.

distractorExplanations.B: These values incorrectly combine the signs instead of subtracting each equilibrium potential.
distractorExplanations.C: Equilibrium potentials alone are not the driving forces; each must be compared with the actual membrane voltage.

learningObjective: Calculate electrochemical driving forces and predict the directions of sodium and potassium flux.

The head is locked to actin because ATP hydrolysis directly causes rigor
Energy from ATP hydrolysis has placed the head in a primed conformation for a subsequent force-generating interaction
ATP hydrolysis has eliminated the need for ATP in further cycles

Smaller increments of whole-muscle force as successive motor units are added
An ability to activate any one fiber independently of its motor neuron
A requirement for all its motor neurons to fire synchronously

The largest units are always recruited first because their axons conduct fastest
All units are recruited at once and force can change only through spike amplitude
Units are recruited in random order independent of excitability

options.text: Every unit must secretly be firing at a tetanizing frequency
Individual muscle action potentials have merged into one larger electrical event
Passive connective tissue generates all of the measured active force
The units fire at different times, allowing their force contributions to overlap

subtopic: Use stimulus interval and twitch duration to compare frequency summation across motor units.

options.text: F, because a shorter twitch guarantees more overlap at the same frequency
Both equally, because only action-potential duration determines mechanical overlap
S, because its next stimulus arrives before the preceding mechanical response ends
Neither, because 20 Hz is below a universal tetanus threshold for every muscle

explanation: The 200 ms twitch outlasts the 50 ms interval, permitting mechanical summation. This predicts overlap, not necessarily complete fusion.

prompt: After a long rest, a single isolated motor axon is stimulated supramaximally at fixed intervals, activating the same motor unit each time. The muscle is held at a fixed length. options.text: Fused tetanus, because successive tension records never relax
The staircase effect, or treppe, in successive discrete twitches
Recruitment of extra motor axons despite the same isolated axon being stimulated
Length-dependent passive tension, even though muscle length and baseline tension remain fixed

explanation: Treppe describes an increase in successive twitch force after rest even when twitches remain discrete; altered calcium availability contributes.

distractorExplanations.A: The stated return to baseline between twitches excludes fused tetanus.

Its active force reaches a maximum because passive stretch is greatest
Its thick filaments shorten to restore overlap without cross-bridge action
Its loss of active force proves that muscle membrane action potentials have failed

The 30 N load produces a lower shortening velocity

subtopic: Predict the force consequence of a changing muscle moment arm at fixed required joint torque.

It remains 150 N because the required torque is unchanged
It rises from 6 N to 12 N
It rises from 150 N to 300 N

explanation: F=torque/moment arm: 6/0.04=150 N and 6/0.02=300 N.

Keep flexion torque unchanged because antagonists cannot act at a stationary joint
Increase flexion torque by 2 N m
Stop using ATP because joint angular velocity is zero

explanation: An added extension torque must be matched by an equal additional flexion torque to preserve zero net torque.

subject: physiology
subtopic: Identify phosphocreatine as an immediate ATP-regeneration buffer during brief intense contraction.
prompt: During the first seconds of a brief maximal contraction, stored ATP alone is inadequate to sustain the demand. Which reaction provides the most immediate buffer for rapid ATP regeneration?

options.text: Oxidative phosphorylation using fatty acids as fuel
Transfer of high-energy phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP
Anaerobic glycolytic ATP formation from stored glycogen
Mitochondrial oxidation of pyruvate to support ATP formation

explanation: Phosphocreatine rapidly donates high-energy phosphate to rephosphorylate ADP, supplementing the small ATP store.

distractorExplanations.A: Fatty-acid oxidation can sustain activity but does not match the immediate rate of phosphate transfer from the phosphocreatine buffer.
distractorExplanations.C: Glycolysis contributes rapidly and overlaps with other systems, but phosphocreatine provides the more immediate phosphate buffer.

subtopic: Distinguish small immediate energy stores from ongoing oxidative ATP supply during sustained muscle activity.
prompt: A postural muscle must sustain repeated activity for a long period with adequate oxygen delivery. Which energy-supply statement best explains why its work can continue after the small phosphocreatine store is no longer sufficient?

options.text: Oxidative metabolism provides continuing ATP resynthesis from available fuels
Stored ATP is normally enough to maintain maximal contraction for several hours
The contractile proteins stop requiring ATP once the first twitch has occurred
Anaerobic glycolysis can indefinitely sustain maximal output without accumulating metabolites

explanation: Sustained muscle activity depends heavily on oxidative ATP production; ATP and phosphocreatine stores alone are small.

distractorExplanations.B: The directly stored ATP supply supports only a very brief period of maximal demand.
distractorExplanations.C: Cross-bridge cycling and calcium handling continue to require ATP during repeated activity.
distractorExplanations.D: Glycolysis is useful for rapid ATP provision but cannot sustain indefinitely the same maximal output without metabolic limitations.

learningObjective: Distinguish small immediate energy stores from ongoing oxidative ATP supply during sustained muscle activity.

subtopic: Interpret preserved muscle electrical excitation during fatigue without attributing all force loss to one unmeasured mechanism.
prompt: An isolated motor unit is stimulated repeatedly through its motor axon. After prolonged intense stimulation, its force declines, but every nerve stimulus still evokes normal muscle action potentials in the tested fibers. Which conclusion is justified by those observations alone?

options.text: The muscle cannot be fatigued because every action potential is normal
Failure of motor-axon conduction has been proved
Complete exhaustion of acetylcholine release is the only possible cause
A limitation downstream of membrane excitation can reduce force despite preserved action potentials

explanation: Contractile and metabolic processes can limit force after excitation. The observations do not by themselves establish one specific biochemical cause.

distractorExplanations.A: Normal action potentials do not guarantee normal calcium handling, cross-bridge performance, or metabolic support.
distractorExplanations.B: Normal recorded muscle spikes show that muscle excitation is occurring in the tested fibers.
distractorExplanations.C: Complete transmitter failure would not account for normal nerve-evoked muscle spikes; force loss has several possible causes.

learningObjective: Interpret preserved muscle electrical excitation during fatigue without attributing all force loss to one unmeasured mechanism.

A primary group Ia ending with a strong dynamic response and a continuing static response
A group II ending that reports only the rate of stretch and stops firing once length is held
A group II ending whose defining response is a brief, strong velocity burst

explanation: Primary Ia endings strongly report rapid change of length and also contribute to the maintained static response after stretch stops.

It produces all of the muscle's external force by shortening the spindle capsule
It converts group Ia sensory axons into motor axons
It silences all spindle feedback so voluntary movement cannot be opposed

It must turn into a group Ib signal because the tendon is fixed
It must decrease because gamma axons directly inhibit every sensory ending
It can increase because contraction of the intrafusal ends stretches the central sensory region

Group Ib afferent, inhibitory interneuron, then reduced alpha-motor discharge
Group Ia afferent through a dorsal root, direct excitation of an alpha motor neuron, then motor output through a ventral root
Group II afferent, mandatory relay through the cerebral cortex, then alpha-motor output

A cutaneous pain receptor activated by every normal tendon tap
